Empirical Research Plan: “China Shock, Innovation, IT Adoption and Productivity in UK Firms, 1996-2007”

────────────────────────────────────────
1. Identification Strategy
────────────────────────────────────────
Preferred strategy: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with a staggered-intensity (“dose–response”) treatment, implemented at the firm-year level:

  • Cross-sectional variation: industries differed markedly in pre-2001 exposure to Chinese import competition and in the post-2001 surge.  
  • Time variation: the WTO accession of China in late-2001 generated a sharp, plausibly exogenous break in the growth rate of Chinese exports.

We will estimate  

 y fit = β (ChinaExp_j × Post_t) + γ_f + δ_t + X’_fit θ + ε_fit,  

where ChinaExp_j is the pre-period (e.g. 1996-2000 mean) share of Chinese imports in UK domestic absorption of industry j, Post_t = 1{t ≥ 2002}.  
β captures the causal effect of an additional unit of exposure on the outcome (log patents, log IT capital, or TFP).

Extensions
• Dynamic event-study coefficients to test parallel trends.  
• Two-stage least squares using a shift-share instrument (Chinese exports to other high-income countries) to address the possible endogeneity of UK-specific import penetration.

────────────────────────────────────────
2. Treatment and Control
────────────────────────────────────────
Treatment variable (“dose”)
   TREAT_jt ≡ Chinese imports to the UK in industry j, divided by UK domestic absorption in j (imports + shipments – exports). Continuous; higher values = higher treatment intensity.

Treatment timing
   Event date = 2002 (first full calendar year after China’s WTO entry, Dec-2001). Post_t = 1 for 2002-2007; 0 for 1996-2001.

Control group
   Firms in industries with low predicted exposure (lower quartile of 1996-2000 China import share). They experience the same macro shocks but far weaker treatment intensity, providing the counterfactual path.

Instrument (for IV robustness)
   Z_jt = Chinese exports to OECD-ex-UK in industry j ÷ OECD domestic absorption. Standard Autor-Dorn-Hanson shift-share design.

No RDD needed; no single cutoff.

────────────────────────────────────────
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
────────────────────────────────────────
A1. Parallel Trends: Absent China’s WTO shock, outcomes of high- and low-exposed industries would have evolved similarly.  
   Plausibility: Pre-2001 growth rates in UK innovation and productivity across industries were largely driven by EU/US demand and ICT diffusion, not by China. We will test via event-study pre-coefficients.

A2. Exogeneity of Chinese Supply Shock: China’s WTO entry and ensuing productivity improvements were driven by internal reforms and global demand, not by UK-industry-specific conditions.  
   Plausibility: Highly believable; UK accounts for a small share of China’s exports.

A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA): One industry’s import exposure does not directly affect another’s innovation path except through general equilibrium channels already captured by year dummies.  
   Plausibility: Some concerns via input-output linkages; we will test robustness controlling for downstream exposure.

A4. No Anticipation: Firms did not substantially adjust innovation in advance of WTO entry because the magnitude/timing were uncertain. Plausible.

────────────────────────────────────────
4. Threats to Identification & Remedies
────────────────────────────────────────
T1. Pre-existing Differential Trends  
   • Remedy: Plot event-study coefficients (1996-2001) ; include industry-specific linear trends; difference-in-differences on growth rates.

T2. Endogenous Firm Composition (exit/entry)  
   • Remedy: Estimate on balanced panel; then include entrants/exits and run inverse probability weighting; check robustness using firm-exit hazard as separate outcome.

T3. Measurement Error in Import Penetration (industry misclassification)  
   • Remedy: Construct exposure with alternative concordances (SIC-CN 2-digit vs 4-digit); instrument with Chinese exports to OECD; cluster SEs at the industry level.

────────────────────────────────────────
5. R Code Outline
────────────────────────────────────────
```r
# ----------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# ----------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast high-dim FE + IV
library(ggplot2)
library(ivreg)       # optional
# ----------------------------------------------------
# 1. Data Loading
# ----------------------------------------------------
firms   <- fread("uk_firm_panel_1996_2007.csv")    # firm-year data
imports <- fread("china_imports_by_industry.csv")  # HS-SIC matched
oecdimp <- fread("china_exports_OECD_notUK.csv")   # instrument

# ----------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable Construction
# ----------------------------------------------------
# Merge exposure at 2-digit SIC level
firms[, sic2 := substr(industry_sic, 1, 2)]
imports[, sic2 := substr(sic, 1, 2)]

# Chinese import penetration = imports / absorption
imports[, pen_china := cn_imports_uk / domestic_absorption]

# Instrumental variable
oecdimp[, sic2 := substr(sic, 1, 2)]
oecdimp[, pen_oecd := cn_exports_oecd / oecd_absorption]

# Bring to firm panel
setkey(firms, sic2, year)
setkey(imports, sic2, year)
setkey(oecdimp, sic2, year)

firms <- imports[firms]
firms <- oecdimp[firms]

# Pre-period average exposure (1996-2000) for shift-share DID
firms[, pre_pen := mean(pen_china[year <= 2000]), by = sic2]

# Post dummy
firms[, post := as.integer(year >= 2002)]

# Outcomes
firms[, ln_patents := log(1 + patent_count)]
firms[, ln_IT      := log(1 + IT_capital)]
firms[, ln_TFP     := log(TFP)]

# Controls (size, capital, age)
firms[, ln_emp  := log(employment)]
firms[, age     := year - birth_year]

# ----------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main DID Specification
# ----------------------------------------------------
did_formula <- ln_patents ~ pre_pen*post + ln_emp + age | firm_id + year
did_pat  <- feols(did_formula, data = firms, cluster = "sic2")
did_it   <- feols(update(did_formula, ln_IT ~ .),  data = firms, cluster = "sic2")
did_tfp  <- feols(update(did_formula, ln_TFP ~ .), data = firms, cluster = "sic2")

etable(list(did_pat, did_it, did_tfp),
       tex = FALSE, dict = c(pre_pen:post = "Exposure × Post"))

# ----------------------------------------------------
# 4. Event-Study
# ----------------------------------------------------
# Create relative year dummies -5…+5
firms[, rel_year := pmin(5, pmax(-5, year - 2001))]
for (k in -5:5) firms[, paste0("D", k) := as.integer(rel_year == k)]

es_form <- ln_TFP ~ i(rel_year, pre_pen, ref = -1) + ln_emp + age | firm_id + year
es_tfp  <- feols(es_form, data = firms, cluster = "sic2")
iplot(es_tfp)

# ----------------------------------------------------
# 5. IV Robustness
# ----------------------------------------------------
iv_formula <- ln_TFP ~ post*pre_pen + ln_emp + age | firm_id + year | (post*pre_pen ~ post*pen_oecd)
iv_tfp <- feols(iv_formula, data = firms, cluster = "sic2")
summary(iv_tfp)
```

────────────────────────────────────────
6. Expected Results
────────────────────────────────────────
Economic theory yields two competing forces: (i) competition discourages slack and pushes firms to innovate (“escaping competition” effect); (ii) import competition can erode cash-flows, reducing resources for R&D.

Given UK’s advanced economy and ample access to capital, I expect the first effect to dominate:

  • A one-standard-deviation (≈4 p.p.) rise in Chinese import penetration increases patents by ≈2–3 %, IT capital by ≈3–4 %, and raises TFP by ≈0.5–1 % over 5 years.

────────────────────────────────────────
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment
────────────────────────────────────────
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable)

C1 Parallel trends verified (pre-coefficients flat?)……………… 0.8  
C2 Treatment exogenous to UK industry shocks…………………… 1.0  
C3 No spillovers across industries (SUTVA)………………………… 0.6  
C4 No simultaneous policy confounders………………………………… 0.7  
C5 Stable composition & no attrition bias…………………………… 0.6  

Overall, the design is credible but hinges on the strength of the parallel-trends evidence and on guarding against compositional changes.
